newsitem.title: USA: New Mexico nuclear dump poses little risk - report.
newsitem.headline: New Mexico nuclear dump poses little risk - report.

text.p: A dump site for medium-grade radioactive waste in salt caverns in southeastern New Mexico poses minimal risks for the next 10,000 years unless it is breached by humans, a panel of experts said in a report released Wednesday.

The National Research Council, an independent research body chartered by Congress, put its stamp of approval on the likely safety of the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant (WIPP) to store contaminated protective clothing, laboratory equipment and machine parts used to make nuclear weapons.
"Provided the WIPP repository is sealed effectively and undisturbed by human activity, the committee knows of no credible or probable scenario for release of radionuclides," the study said.

The WIPP project to store contaminated materials now held at various Energy Department former weapons plants, has been in the works for 20 years, but the facility completed almost 10 years ago near Carlsbad, New Mexico, has yet to open.
Assistant Energy Secretary Al Alm said in a telephone news conference the National Research Council report "gives the public confidence that this repository can be safely operated."
"To the extent that we don't have a safe repository, we have the waste at several points around the country with many more people potentially exposed," Alm said.

Don Hancock, of the Southwest Research and Information Center, said the report still did not answer questions about water flow at the site, as well as potential effects of drastic climate change that could occur within 10,000 years.
The Energy Department selected the site and built the facility without fully gauging potential flaws, he said.

Since then the department has tried to change the regulations it would operate under instead of addressing fundamental problems, said Hancock, whose research organization has sued to block the project.
Hancock also questioned the timing of the report's release, a week before the Energy Department is to apply to the Environmental Protection Agency for an environmental compliance certificate.
"It was totally political timing," he said of the study.

The National Research Council said its analysis indicated that the WIPP "has the ability to isolate transuranic waste for more than 10,000 years, provided it remain undisturbed by human activity," and it said speculation about far-off human activity should not be the main basis for judging its safety.

While critics have said mining and drilling for nearby deposits of oil, natural gas and potash increased risk of intrusion, the panel of scientists said such risks were overstated because the resources will be practically exhausted in less than 100 years.
